case_study_insert.main_stem: ClearScan Diagnostics (CSD) is a private limited company in the healthcare diagnostics sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2008 by Dr Priya Nair, it runs three imaging centres and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. CSD plans to invest $890,000 in a new MRI scanner and telemedicine reporting hub, financed by a $500,000 ten-year bank loan and a $390,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $450,000 a year, a variable cost of $48 a unit and a selling price of $138 for a diagnostic scan, and currently performs 12,000 units a year. CSD faces two problems: a 3.2% scan retake rate and rising patient complaints about report delays.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: The scanning centres performed 2,900 scans in December with a 3.2% retake rate, down from 5.1% a year earlier. Patient complaints about report delays rose from 22 to 41 per month. Average report turnaround is 3.7 days. A survey of 450 patients found that 73% would pay $20 more for same-day digital reports, and 56% choose a provider on the speed of results. 14 of 52 radiographers have not completed on-the-job training on the new MRI scanner; a vendor certification course costs $760 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of ClearScan Diagnostics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as CSD's $500,000 scanner loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.4% from $13.00 to $13.70 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for radiography and administrative staff. (3) Medical consumables and imaging contrast import costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while private healthcare spending grew 3.9% over the same period.

questions.question_text: CSD plans to fund part of its $890,000 scanner investment with a $500,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CSD of raising the $390,000 through a share issue instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $390,000 share issue provides equity that requires no interest or capital repayment, so CSD avoids extra debt service on top of the $500,000 loan while meeting fixed costs of $450,000 a year. The money can be spent on the telemedicine reporting hub and on reducing the 3.7-day report turnaround, rather than being paid to a lender as finance charges on the $890,000 investment.

Point 2: Equity improves resilience if the 3.2% retake rate delays scans and depresses revenue below the current 12,000 units, because there is no fixed repayment that could trigger a liquidity crisis. It also spreads the risk of the new MRI scanner among investors rather than leaving Dr Priya Nair's original centres wholly exposed to the bank. A larger loan would demand repayments whether or not the telemedicine hub reduces the 41 monthly complaints, whereas equity gives CSD time to establish the service. New shareholders may also bring healthcare contacts that help CSD win referrals to the three imaging centres.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CSD's investment, complaints and costs.

questions.question_text: CSD's report-delivery complaints rose from 22 to 41 a month. Consider recruiting extra radiographers, a telemedicine reporting partnership, or automated reporting software. Which should CSD choose to cut the 3.7-day report turnaround? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Recruiting extra radiographers: More staff would directly reduce the backlog behind the 3.7-day turnaround and the 41 monthly complaints. However, recruitment and salaries add to fixed costs of $450,000 a year, and with 14 of 52 radiographers still needing scanner training, new hires would also require costly induction before becoming productive.

Telemedicine reporting partnership: Sending scans to specialist radiologists abroad could give same-day digital reports, matching the 73% of 450 surveyed patients who would pay $20 more and the 56% who choose on speed. It converts a fixed staffing cost into a variable one and can flex with the 12,000-scan volume, but it depends on reliable data links and may reduce control over quality and the 3.2% retake rate.

Automated reporting software: Software could triage normal scans and issue routine reports instantly, cutting turnaround without the ongoing salary cost of new hires. It fits the $890,000 technology investment and supports the 73% premium for same-day reports, but it requires validation, may not handle complex cases, and does not by itself fix radiographer shortages.

A partnership also avoids the 14 radiographer training gap becoming a bottleneck, because reporting capacity can be bought in while local staff are upskilled.

Recommendation: CSD should choose the telemedicine reporting partnership, supported by automated software for routine scans. Together they deliver the same-day reports the survey values and cut the 3.7-day wait without permanently raising fixed costs. Recruitment is rejected because it adds long-term salary costs on top of $450,000 fixed costs and training needs; software alone is rejected because it cannot cover complex scans or the full backlog.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the options with minimal reference to CSD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CSD with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why recruitment and software alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: CSD uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. Explain two benefits for CSD of this approach in reducing its 3.2% scan retake rate and 41 monthly complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 52 radiographers to suggest improvements to scanning protocols, which is valuable when the retake rate is 3.2% and 41 patients a month complain about delays Staff who perform the scans daily can identify avoidable retakes, and involving them builds commitment to the new MRI scanner, helping CSD sustain the fall from 5.1% and meet the 73% demand for same-day reports.

Point 2: A hierarchical structure provides a clear chain of command for quality checks and for escalating report delays, so responsibility for the 3.7-day turnaround is explicit. Defined roles also support training of the 14 radiographers new to the scanner, making it easier to standardise technique and protect the 56% of patients who choose a provider on speed of results. Consulting the 52 staff also makes the change to same-day digital reports easier to implement, since the radiographers who must deliver the 3.7-day turnaround are more likely to support a system they helped design.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CSD's retake rate, complaints and training needs.

questions.question_text: CSD must train 14 of 52 radiographers on the new MRI scanner. Consider on-the-job training or a vendor certification course at $760 per employee. Which should CSD choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the scanner is directly relevant to CSD's own equipment, costs no fees, and keeps all 14 radiographers scanning the 12,000 units a year, which matters while the 3.7-day report turnaround and 41 monthly complaints already strain the service. It also lets experienced staff demonstrate techniques that reduce the 3.2% retake rate. The drawbacks are that trainers are productive radiographers whose own work slows, practice may vary, and no external certificate is issued.

Vendor certification course: At $760 per radiographer, certifying all 14 costs $10,640 (14 × $760), modest against the $890,000 scanner investment. It gives structured technical training and a recognised certificate that supports quality assurance, and removes staff from the scanning schedule so learning is uninterrupted. However, it takes 14 of 52 radiographers away from three centres temporarily, which could lengthen the 3.7-day turnaround, and generic content may need on-site follow-up.

There is a further quality argument: a recognised certificate may reassure referring clinicians about the new scanner, yet with 41 complaints a month the immediate priority is report speed, which on-the-job training protects better. The $10,640 fee would also have to come from a budget already stretched by the $450,000 fixed costs and the $500,000 loan.

Decision: CSD should choose on-the-job training first, with short vendor certification later for lead radiographers. On-the-job training protects scanning capacity when reports are already delayed, is free and is machine-specific; full vendor training is rejected because withdrawing 14 radiographers would worsen the 41-complaint problem and the $10,640 fee duplicates skills best learned on the scanner.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CSD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of CSD's delays and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and scanner relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CSD's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $450,000 ÷ ($138 − $48) = $450,000 ÷ $90 = 5,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 5,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $138 − $48 = $90. Answer: contribution per unit is $90.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CSD's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 5,000-unit break-even output with 12,000 scans performed shows a margin of safety of 7,000 units, giving confidence to install the new MRI scanner and telemedicine hub.
2. Contribution of $90 a scan lets managers assess the $20 same-day report premium; it would lift contribution to $110 on those scans and show how many extra patients are needed to cover $450,000 fixed costs.
3. With fixed costs of $450,000 and contribution of $90, managers can set the scan volume needed to service the $500,000 loan before committing further capital.
4. Average total cost ($450,000 ÷ 12,000 + $48 = $85.50) can be tracked quarterly to detect waste from the 3.2% retake rate and to judge whether the 10.8% consumables inflation is being controlled.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 5,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $90 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 12,000-unit output; $20 premium modelling; loan-service volume for the $500,000 loan; and average total cost of $85.50 to monitor retakes and consumables inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CSD's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CSD's performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 50.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: 2024: 1,350 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 45.0%; 450 ÷ 3,000 × 100 = 15.0%; 450 ÷ 2,500 × 100 = 18.0%. 2025: 1,800 ÷ 3,600 × 100 = 50.0%; 720 ÷ 3,600 × 100 = 20.0%; 720 ÷ 3,200 × 100 = 22.5%. Revenue rose to $3,600,000 while cost of sales increased only to $1,800,000, so the first margin widened; operating profit reached $720,000. Capital employed grew to $3,200,000, yet the return on that larger base improved, and interest payable fell from $60,000 to $50,000.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The rise from 45.0% to 50.0% shows CSD is controlling the direct costs of scanning despite 10.8% consumables inflation. The jump from 15.0% to 20.0% indicates fixed costs of $450,000 are being spread over more of the 12,000 scans, helped by lower interest charges. The return on capital employed improving from 18.0% to 22.5% is the strongest evidence because it shows the enlarged $3,200,000 asset base is generating more profit, supporting the $890,000 scanner purchase. A caveat is that no receivables or cash data are provided, so stronger profitability does not prove CSD can meet short-term debts; the $500,000 loan still requires repayment.

Conclusion: CSD's performance has improved. All three measures rose, and the 22.5% return on capital employed confirms that investment is adding value rather than merely expanding revenue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate percentage calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CSD of charging the $20 premium for same-day digital reports identified in its patient survey.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 450 patients found that 73% would pay $20 more for same-day digital reports and 56% choose a provider on speed of results, so the premium could lift the $138 selling price toward $158 and raise contribution per scan from $90 to $110. That extra contribution would help cover fixed costs of $450,000 a year, service the $500,000 scanner loan and fund the telemedicine reporting hub.

Disadvantage: charging more may deter the patients who cannot afford the premium, and with 41 complaints a month about report delays a higher price could increase dissatisfaction if the 3.7-day turnaround is not cut first. If only a minority take up same-day reporting, CSD may gain little revenue while still needing to invest in faster systems, and the 3.2% retake rate could absorb any extra contribution. CSD should first demonstrate that the 3.7-day turnaround has fallen, otherwise charging more for speed may damage the 56% of patients who choose on speed of results.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CSD's survey, contribution and service problems.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 5.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in medical consumables costs will affect CSD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If CSD's $500,000 ten-year scanner loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $450,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the immediate effect is zero. Higher rates could make future borrowing for the $890,000 hub more expensive and slightly reduce private demand, but CSD can cap this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.4%, to $13.70 an hour): With a workforce of 52, including administrative and support staff, this raises wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be invented. The honest comparison is productivity: 12,000 units ÷ 52 staff = 230.8 scans per worker, so the rise is sustainable only if output per worker holds or grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $90 contribution per scan is squeezed, especially while retakes waste time.

Medical consumables inflation (10.8%): The $48 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8% it would add 0.108 × $48 = $5.18 per scan; at 12,000 scans that is $62,208 a year. This cuts the $90 contribution on every scan, and the 3.2% retake rate multiplies usage, though the $20 same-day premium and 3.9% growth in private healthcare spending provide some recovery.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in medical consumables has the greatest impact. It compounds across all 12,000 scans and directly erodes the $90 contribution that justifies the $890,000 investment, and retakes amplify it; the interest rise is only $3,750 a year and the wage effect, though real, cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity and the premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to CSD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on CSD's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that consumables inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
